newsitem.title: USA: Hair-eating doll to carry warning label.
newsitem.headline: Hair-eating doll to carry warning label.

text.p: Battery-operated Cabbage Patch dolls blamed for chewing on the hair and fingers of at least 35 children will now carry a warning label, the Consumer Product Safety Commission announced Tuesday.

The manufacturer of the Cabbage Patch Snacktime Kids doll, Mattel Inc, agreed to attach a warning to all dolls still on store shelves and on all future production following reports of children getting their hair and fingers caught in its mouth, the CPSC said in a written sattement.
Mattel has distributed 700,000 Snacktime Kids since August 1996. The doll has a battery-operated mouth and is supposed to eat plastic celery sticks.
The CPSC and Mattel were aware of 35 incidents where a child's hair or finger was trapped in the doll's mouth, the statement said. No serious injuries have been reported.

"The information will warn that long hair and fingers can get caught in the doll's mouth and will tell consumers that the doll's chewing action can be stopped immediately by removing the backpack. The doll will not operate without the backpack in place," the CPSC said.

Mattel's senior vice president for communications, Glen Bozarth, said the company was deeply concerned by the safety complaints and announced that Mattel had set up a hotline (1-800-524-TOYS) to provide consumers with the safety information and warnings.
The CPSC said both the agency and Mattel were pursuing separate investigations of possible safety risks posed by the doll.

Four-year-old Emily Newton, of Tavares, Fla., was the latest victim of the hair-eating doll. Her mother reported Monday that a Cabbage Patch Snacktime Kid gnawed on an 8-inch strand of her daughter's waist-length hair, but was pried off without injury to Emily.
In other incidents, children have lost hair or the dolls have had to be dismantled before giving up their grip on the child's hair.
